text: István Maruzs / Age: 41
Rank/Position: Private (reservist), trench runner / messenger
Civilian Occupation: Farmer
Origin: Nógrád County, Northern Hungary
Maruzs István simply couldn't understand why everyone else wasn't enjoying this
at least half as much as he was.
Sure, the cold was miserable.
The food was scarce, and what there was tasted like horse dung.
But those were minor inconveniences compared to the fact
that he was finally allowed to hold a weapon. A real weapon.
One he could actually use. And not just for shooting at targets.
But for killing a man.
Because István had fantasized about taking a human life for as long as he could remember.
He could never put into words what was so seductive about it.
It wasn't the cruelty of the ritual.
He didn't take pleasure in someone else's pain.
What fascinated him was the idea itself. The switch.
That a person who existed could suddenly stop existing — because of him.
The biggest obstacle, for years, was the law.
He was terrified of it. Not of morality. Of consequences.
Of what would happen to him if he did what he wanted to do.
So he stayed inert. He dreamed. He imagined.
And he did nothing.
Sometimes he went hunting with his friend, Endre.
But shooting a pheasant or a rabbit did nothing to ease the itch
that took up most of his waking life.
He liked pig slaughters better.
There was something almost human in a pig's eyes.
If nothing else, it gave him a taste of the forbidden fruit.
Then, about five years ago, luck smiled at him — briefly.
István lived off farming.
They had a few plots of land, part of his wife's dowry.
But his father-in-law could never bring himself to trust him with the work.
He couldn't believe István was capable of dealing with it alone.
So he would come out with him, again and again, to work the soil.
And he would wear István down with his chatter.
One of his favorite topics was his broken heart.
The tragedy that István and Marika — István's wife —
hadn't given him a strong, beautiful grandchild.
Not even a weak, ugly one. Simply none.
On that wonderful day, he was complaining about it again.
István was already forming a fake excuse in his mind.
He was going to say something and go home. Anything to get away.
But he didn't get the chance.
His father-in-law started shaking. His whole body seized.
And then he simply toppled into the furrow the plow had cut into the earth.
István ran to him.
At first, fear crushed his chest in an iron grip.
Then, as he watched the old man convulse in the dirt, foam at the mouth,
something else replaced it. Relief.
A kind of calm he had wanted his entire life —
but had never dared to hope he would actually feel.
He positioned the oxen and the plow so they would block the view from the neighboring fields,
in case anyone looked over.
Then he sat down on the ground. And he watched his father-in-law die.
It was a long process. Painful, surely, for the older man.
During it, István even experimented.
He wanted to know what would happen if he pinched the man's nose shut.
As it turned out, not much — except that the old man drowned faster
in the thick, wet sludge rising in his throat.
Only when István was certain there was no pulse left did he start yelling for help.
With all that in mind, it's no surprise that István was almost the only man
whose face shone on the day of conscription.
Luckily, people read his eagerness as patriotism, so they didn't ask questions.
Unluckily, once they reached the Voronezh region,
he was assigned as a trench runner. A courier.
So he spent his days sprinting from point A to point B with messages,
while everyone else got to do the part that mattered.
Shooting. Killing.
He was already flirting with the idea of disobeying orders
when the platoon commander took pity on him.
By January fifth — without the German support they'd been promised —
the situation against the Soviet superiority had been judged so desperate
that every able-bodied man was handed a rifle and pushed to the lip of the trench.
When István received his weapon, he broke into a wide grin.
The platoon commander looked at him with fatherly pride.
He patted his shoulder.
And in a voice thick with emotion, he said only this:
“Now that's a patriot right here!”
